items.markdown:
Recovering requirements from legacy code means `acting as an archaeologist to reverse-engineer hidden business rules, data flows, and edge cases when documentation is missing or outdated`.

### Step-by-Step Recovery Process

- **Black-Box Exploration (Behavioral Analysis):** Run the software with sample inputs, vary parameters, and observe outputs or side effects (like database changes or log files) to map out what the system *actually* does rather than what it was supposed to do.[[1]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=omLzvQqbxo8)
- **Capture and Replay Testing:** Record real-world or sample input/output pairs using command-line scripts or automated harnesses. Replay these inputs to establish a baseline safety net before you touch anything.[[1]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=omLzvQqbxo8)
- **Static Code Analysis:** Use automated tools or IDE navigation (call hierarchies, cross-references) to trace entry points, API routes, database queries, and conditional (`if/else` ) branching logic.[[1]](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/4760074/advice-on-working-with-legacy-code)[[2]](https://www.scnsoft.com/software-development/about/how-we-work/reverse-engineering)
- **Domain & Data Mapping:** Inspect database schemas, stored procedures, and serialization models. The shape of the database often reveals the true, unstated business requirements better than the application layer does.
- **Trace Git/VCS History:** Dig through old commit logs, pull requests, and ticket references. Often, commit messages explain *why* a bizarre workaround or hack was introduced.[[1]](https://dev.to/adedaniel/dealing-with-legacy-code-as-an-engineer-261d)
- **Interview Stakeholders and Users:** Talk to long-tenured employees, customer support, or power users who rely on the quirks of the system daily to validate whether an observed behavior is a feature or a bug.[[1]](https://dev.to/madza/how-do-you-deal-with-legacy-projects-72j)

### Best Practices to Avoid Breaking Things

- **Isolate before you change:** Wrap legacy modules or write characterization tests (tests that capture current behavior, even if it is weird) before attempting refactoring.[[1]](https://www.cubicfox.com/blog/strategies-for-dealing-with-legacy-code)[[2]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=omLzvQqbxo8)
- **Incremental extraction:** Pull small, self-contained functions or business rules out of massive "god classes" piece by piece.[[1]](https://medium.com/legacycode/5-ways-to-work-with-legacy-code-53c93b55b715)[[2]](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/4760074/advice-on-working-with-legacy-code)
- **Document as you go:** Convert your discoveries into living documentation (e.g., Markdown ADRs, updated specs, or automated unit tests) so the next engineer does not have to repeat the archaeology.[[1]](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/4760074/advice-on-working-with-legacy-code)

If you'd like to dive deeper, tell me:

- **What programming language or framework** is the legacy code written in?
- **What is your main goal** (e.g., writing a bug fix, migrating to a new stack, or writing formal documentation)?

I can give you more specific tools and strategies for your project.
